title: Wat Khao Chong Krachok: 396 Steps to Three-Bay Views
metaDesc: Climb Khao Chong Krachok in Prachuap Khiri Khan, Thailand — 396 steps to a relic chedi and a 360-degree view over three bays, plus how to handle the monkeys, when to go, and how to get there.

h1:
Wat Khao Chong Krachok
396 Steps to the Three-Bay View
intro: Khao Chong Krachok is a small hill right in the middle of Prachuap town, the kind everyone can spot from the streets below. A flight of 396 steps takes you up to a chedi holding Buddha relics at the summit, where the view opens onto three curving bays all around you. Monkeys greet you along the way (and try to swipe your stuff), and locals treat the hill as the symbol of their town.

blocks.html: If you're in Prachuap with time for just one spot in town, plenty of people will tell you to climb Khao Chong Krachok, because it rolls a temple visit, a bit of exercise, and a sea view into one. The summit sits around 245 metres above sea level, and 396 steps gets you there — not far, but enough to leave you a little winded. At the top is Wat Khao Chong Krachok, home to Buddha relics that King Rama IX came to enshrine here in 1958, along with a replica Buddha footprint.

blocks.text: What climbing the 396 steps is like

blocks.html: The 396 steps are concrete the whole way, with handrails on both sides and rest pavilions at intervals where you can catch your breath. Most people make the climb comfortably in about 15–25 minutes, depending on how often you stop. The view opens up bit by bit as you go, and as you near the top you start to see the bay below — a spot where people love to pause for photos. If your knees aren't great, just take it slow; nobody's rushing you.

items: Footwear — wear sneakers or shoes you can walk in easily; some sections of the stairs are fairly steep.
Water — bring some up with you, as there aren't many shops at the top.
Dress — it's a temple, so dress reasonably modestly since you'll be paying respects at the summit.

blocks.html: Khao Chong Krachok has a lot of monkeys, especially around the lower part of the stairs. The ones here are used to people and pretty bold — they like to grab plastic bags, water bottles, or any food you're carrying in your hand. At some points you can rent a monkey-deterrent stick for around 50 THB, so if you're nervous it's worth having one for peace of mind. But most of the time, simply not flashing a bag around is enough to get you through.

blocks.title: Handling the monkeys without the drama
blocks.html: Tuck snacks and water bottles away in a zipped bag, don't swing a plastic bag back and forth, don't hold eye contact with a monkey for too long, and never feed them — the more you give, the more they swarm in. If a monkey walks up close, just calmly step around it and don't run.

blocks.text: The three-bay view at the top

blocks.html: What makes people willing to climb is the 360-degree view at the summit, looking out over three curving bays lined up in a row — which is why locals call it the three-bay viewpoint: Ao Prachuap, Ao Manao, and Ao Noi, with small islands scattered across the sea. On a clear day the curve of the coastline looks gorgeous, and it's the angle you'll come across most often when you search for photos of Prachuap online.

items.name: Ao Prachuap
items.blurb: The town-centre bay that stands out most from the summit, with a beachfront road and the town stretching along it.

items.name: Ao Manao
items.blurb: The southern bay inside the Wing 5 air base, with clear water and a clean beach — another popular spot in town.

items.name: Ao Noi
items.blurb: The quieter northern bay, with a fishing village and Khao Ta Mong Lai nearby.

blocks.text: When to go and how to get there

blocks.html: The times people most like to climb are early morning and the late afternoon before sunset, when the sun isn't harsh and the view is at its best. Going midday means more heat and a tougher climb. The hill sits right in the middle of Prachuap town and is easy to reach — visitors usually park near Wat Thammikaram Worawihan across the way and walk over to the foot of the stairs. There's no entrance fee, but if you'd like to make a donation there's a box at the top.

items: Best times — morning 6:30–8:30, or late afternoon 16:00–18:00 to dodge the midday sun.
Time needed — about 1–1.5 hours up and down, including photos and paying respects.

blocks.title: Pair it with
blocks.html: After coming down the hill, you can wander the market in Prachuap town and find an easy breakfast, or drive on to Ao Manao — the bay you just spotted from the summit. It makes for a tidy half-day trip around town.

faq.q: How many steps does Khao Chong Krachok have, and is the climb tiring?
faq.a: There are 396 concrete steps with handrails and rest pavilions at intervals. Most people climb in about 15–25 minutes. It's fairly tiring but not punishing — kids and older visitors who are up to it can manage as long as they go slowly and rest along the way.

faq.q: Are the monkeys at Khao Chong Krachok aggressive? What should I watch for?
faq.a: The monkeys are used to people and bold about approaching. They like to grab plastic bags, water bottles, and food, so keep your things tucked away in a bag, don't swing a bag around, don't feed them, and don't hold eye contact too long. You can rent a monkey-deterrent stick for around 50 THB at the foot of the hill if you're worried.

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee to climb Khao Chong Krachok?
faq.a: There's no entrance fee — it's free to climb, with just a donation box at the top for anyone who'd like to give. Visitors usually park near Wat Thammikaram Worawihan across the way and walk over to the foot of the stairs.

faq.q: Which bays make up the three-bay view?
faq.a: From the summit you'll see three curving bays in a row: Ao Prachuap (town centre), Ao Manao (to the south), and Ao Noi (to the north), along with small islands out at sea. It's a 360-degree view that's become the signature of Prachuap town.

faq.q: What's the best time to visit Khao Chong Krachok?
faq.a: Early morning around 6:30–8:30 or late afternoon 16:00–18:00 is best, when the sun is gentler and the view is lovely. Midday is hotter and the climb is harder. Allow about 1–1.5 hours for the climb up and down plus paying respects.
